title: Extended ACLs: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Now meet a stricter guard. They check who you are. Then they check where you're going, and why.

scenes.heading: The embassy checkpoint
scenes.narration: At an embassy, the guard checks more than nationality. They also check which office you want, and what you're there for. In networking, that's the source, the destination and the port. For example, allow staff to reach the visa office, but only for secure web. Block everyone else. Because it can be so specific, an extended list goes close to the source.

scenes.heading: Writing one
scenes.narration: Here's an example. Permit T C P from one network to a server on port four four three. The wildcard masks are inverse masks. And the invisible last line denies everything else.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. Extended lists can match ports and protocols, not just addresses. The wildcard is the inverse of the mask. And a list with only permits still blocks everything else.

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva extended ACL lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Extended lists check source, destination and port. Place them close to the source. And remember the implicit deny at the end. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva extended ACL lab.
